title: The Galton Case
review:
I paid $5 for this book at a thrift store knowing nothing about it. (Except someone recommended me the author a while ago) This is a noir detective book from the 50s originally published as a cheap paperback. These things are meant to be read by men on the bus on the way to work. We got women in tight shirts, gangsters, rich families, a couple action scenes. Your grandparents would've loved this book. Due to this purpose, the book has a kinda odd structure. Each chapter is like 4 pages long and they are all the same. The detective shows up somewhere, talks to a tropey character, and gets information to set up the next location with a new tropey character in it for next chapter. The book always felt in motion, but never felt it was going somewhere interesting. By the end I really liked the story, but I wondered what the purpose was in the middle. I think mostly that was the structure just feeling odd to me. Also the protagonist is nothing. He's not a character. I've previously said the key to a mystery is good characters. That's not the case here, so why did I finish it? Because the prose and theme are really good. We are dealing with a family in shambles because of a rebellious son being cast out of the family. And the book explores the wake this event, all the people hurt and all the people trying to take advantage of it. And these sentences really feel so good to read. It's just cover to cover amazing writing. Actually, here's a bit of writing I just found by flipping to a random page.

“Why did you do it?” I said.

'I don’t know. I guess I just got sick of him. Now it’s time for me to take my punishment. I killed, and I deserve to die.'

The tragic words had an unreal quality. She spoke them like a life-size puppet activated by strings and used by a voice that didn’t belong to her. Only her eyes were her own, and they contained a persistent stunned innocence.

There's really no reason to read this unless you really liked that sentence, or you're an 80 year old detective story fan. I enjoyed it, but I don't think I'll read anything else by this author.

title: There is no Antimemetics Division
review:
This really shows the best parts of SCP. It's so weird and creative. Unlike most horror, this feels like something that could've only been written in the 21st century. It's just so out there.

The book is about 'antimemes', SCPs that remove themselves from your memory. Stuff like The Silence in Doctor Who: when you stop looking at them you immediately forget they ever existed. How do you fight something like that? Answer: be really smart.

Like the best sci-fi novels, every chapter in this book gives an idea that could carry an entire series on its own, and then moves on to something even more crazy and out there. I was really surprised how much ideas kept escalating in this book. Ngl all this escalating probably made this thing hype af to read as it was being released on the SCP wiki back in 2015.

And this book is scary. I got really spooked by it. I had such a good time with this book I finished it in two days. The best SCP authors always have the most inventive stories, and it really pisses me off that more of them havn't made the jump into traditional publishing yet, so it's going to be a while before we get another book like this one again.

title: Shadow and Bone (Shadow and Bone Trilogy: Book 1)
review:
I didn't finish a single book in February, despite reading more total in February than January. And then I finished this book in 4 days. Whoops. But can you blame me? It's a YA novel with two love interests, in a school, with a rags to riches peasant girl. Be still my beating heart!

I'd already read the authors next series (Six of Crows). The setting and plot of this are only 30% as interesting and everything feels more generic. I can't tell if this is just Bardugo in her unformed larval stage, or whether she used something more tried and true to break into the industry? Could be both. Six of Crows was a rag-tag group of people conning their way across the world to do a heist. This is self insert protagonist being the hero of the prophecy and learning to harness her special powers that no one else has. But I still had a great time reading it. If we judge books by whether I finish them Bardugo is a greater writer than Borges, Flannery O'Connor, and C.S. Lewis.

In terms of pure enjoyment, I had a better time reading all four books I started in February vs this one. This one was very easy to read, but it's all in one ear out the other. This book was like popcorn. Maybe the book equivalent is YouTube vs movies. One is just easier to consume for long periods of time.

But lets not forget; this proves you never age out of YA. Hot boys are forever. (And the boys are really hot)

(And for the record, the twist in the 3rd act got me. I predicted it wrong)

title: Project Hail Mary
review:
Im gonna have a hard time watching this movie in a few months because the protagonist in my head looks nothing like Ryan Gosling.

This author is just so wholesome. He just loves science in this pure and amateur way. You know he follows NASA on Twitter and loves talking about fun science facts.

The Martian was just a series of unique science problem -> fun science solution -> problem -> solution etc for thewhole thing. That book was great, but this one's plot has a little more sauce. More character and more emotional moments. Nothing crazy, just more to spice things up. Another big difference from The Martian is this book's science is a lot more out there. For me it was always in the realm of possibility, but there might be a few too many crazy ideas for some people. This book is about 1/3 flashback, especially early on. My theory is the movie is only going to have 3 total flashback scenes.

It was a lot easier and breezy than The Remains of the Day. If you want to get back into reading this might be what gets you started. Fun science romp.

title: The Remains of the Day
review:
This protagonist broke my heart. Stevens is a butler reflecting on his life, and his first person perspective gives the book such an irony. His life is so sad, but he doesn't see it that way. He's actually quite proud of his career, serving the great Lords and Ladies of Britain. But his employers never thank him, and he has paid such a price to do this job well. First off he has no friends. At one point he remarks 'a butler is only off-duty when they are alone.' And the person he most could've become friends with (Miss Kenton) he frequently hurts in unintentional ways because of his devotion to his job. So many times he leaves her in tears and he is wondering why she is so unprofessional. It hurts so much seeing how much he hurts her and he refuses to see he's even done it. The irony of Stevens's life is most obviously seen when we learn his Lord was a Nazi sympathizer in WWII. Stevens was at least taking consolation in serving a great man, except he wasn't. And he seems to have blocked from his mind him being a bad man.

Every time I picked up this book i'd read a section and think 'I have to mention this in the review.' The book is so dense with chapters i'll remember the rest of my life.

This book is so sad, but it doesn't get there by killing baby goats or blowing up orphanages. The painful sorrow is from one guy, talking about his sad life, and being proud of it. There's one heartaching moment near the end where it seems for a second Stevens will learn his lesson, but then he doesn't. This book was beautiful. I see why it won a Nobel Prize in literature.

Blessed Are You
review: I've read this book more times than I can count. It's one of those books where I can pick it up, flip the next page and then sit chewing on just that one page for an hour. Fun fact: my first tattoo was inspired by this book. When eating a fish, it's easy to cut off the big chunks of meat, but it takes serious skill and effort to cleanly debone the fish, taking all of the meat off. (reviewed 6-15-2026)

title: Listening At Prayer
review: This is a very short book on prayer writen by one of the founders of the CFRs, who you might know as a franciscan order known for living in the most rough and poor parts of the world. It's not long, and provides a little perspective I havn't seen even among other franciscan writers. Also like franciscan writing it isn't that deep. It's written by an incredibly holy man, simply. That's the franciscan special. (reviewed 6-15-2026)

title: Happy Are You Poor
review: This is the gold standard for Catholic writing about living 'poverty of spirit'. I say that because it doesn't cop out of that. It really encourages you to strictly examine what's important in your life. (reviewed 6-15-2026)

title: The Fire Within
review: Like Happy are you Poor this is also a gold standard, but for examining the writings of St John of the Cross and especially Theresa of Avila. While Dubay is at his core an academic he doesn't reduce God with his language. Ultimately the reason to read this book is if you want a 500 page book diving into the Interior Mansions and Dark Night of the Soul. If you are interested but don't want to read the whole thing I'd look at the chapter list and skip to what you're most interested in. (reviewed 6-15-2026)

title: Batman: The Killing Joke
review: I read it because I heard this was the most iconic Batman Story. Yeah it's pretty good. The central message is the same as The Joker in Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight Rises. Everyone is just one bad day away from being like the Joker. Joker kidnaps commissioner Gordan and tortures him while Batman is in a race to save him. Did I mention it's also really short? You could read the whole thing in the hour. (reviewed 6-15-2026)

title: Watchmen
review: The funniest thing about Watchmen is if you go on Reddit tons of people rank it as their #1 comic OF ALL TIME. So when people are thinking of getting into comics they find these top 10 lists and decide to read this as their first comic. And many people will tell you it's not a great comic to read as your first comic. I know this all happens because this is what I did./n/nI'm writing this review years after I read it and I can confirm: this is isn't a great place to start. So much of this plays with the tropes of comics, some of which you might absorb from the MCU but most of which you won't. I'm not saying you can't have a good time with this, I did, but you can tell it's meant to be read in conversation with the entire industry./n/nWatchmen is very thoughtful(reviewed 6-15-2026)

title: Steelheart (Reckoners: Book 1)
review: This was the first thing by Brandon Sanderson i'd read. I read it because I wanted something that was like the Boys, but not bad. This was that. It's about evil superheroes being killed by people who don't have powers, but study the heroes to learn their one weakness that turns off their powers Every person they fight has a single question: what do they not want you to know? Does this person always fight at night? Why is their costume like that? Why did they kill this person, did they know something? Everything else I'd come to see as Sanderson's hallmarks are here: plain but effective prose, well explained power systems, some medium-to-good characters, and an absolute cascade of twists, action, and emotion in the finale. (reviewed 6-15-2026)

title: The Way of Kings (Stormlight Archives: Book 1)
review: Sometimes, all it takes to really love a book is the abstract ideas of one of the characters in it. If you've been sold the wants and goals of that character hard enough, it almost doesn't matter the specific plot, you'll be cheering for them the whole time anyway. Kaladin is the hero of this story his dad was a doctor and trained him to be a doctor. But Kaladin wanted to be a solider. That's the intitial tragedy, he was trained to heal but wants to hurt. And then Kaladin is captured and sold as a slave, forced to the lowest level of society because of the choices he made. That abstract concept was strong enough to carry me through the whole book. But that is only one of four main characters of this story. We also have a disgraced aristocrat pretending to be a scholar to steal a jewel from the king's daughter and save her own house. We have an assassin who killed the former king, on the run and tormented by guilt. And finally we have the dead king's brother, old fashioned and obssessed with virtue while the rest of the court plays politics over who will be the next king. You see, this is the beginnning of Sanderson's giant epic-scale fantasy story. This is his Wheel of Time, his Elric, his Lord of the Rings. However, in the years since reading this I've wondered if Sanderson's talents are not best used in that level of storytelling./n/nThere's a lot going on here, and Sanderson starts off his epic story well, but I think this book is good despite being a fantasy epic. If this story focused on just two characters I think the story would be stronger. The other stories aren't even bad, I think portions of Kaladin's story are actually kinda boring, and at those points the other characters are at the most interesting parts of their story, so everything stays exciting the whole way through. Despite my criticism, when I'd first read this book I called it my favorite book of all time. The issues with this series wouldn't be seen for me until the later books. (reviewed 6-15-2026)

title: Words of Radiance (Stormlight Archives: Book 2)
review: This is considered by fans the greatest of the series, and I can see why but this is where the cracks started to show for me. I was getting tired of the story being dragged down by the worst of the plots happening at that given moment. Something I do really like in this one is that the protagonists start interacting with each other. We see how other characters see Kaladin and vice versa. The cast all has very different views of each other and it brought a smile to my face every time we'd see it happen. But parts of this book drag. Sanderson loves to build up to his extremely high climaxes, which are very exciting, but the buildup can be quite bad. I'm not even against slow pacing, it's just that nothing interesting is talked about or done during the low points. This book has some great highs (Kaladin jumping in to save Adolin while he is dueling for the Shardplate is a standout for me), but when we are building up it feels pretty lackluster. Also I heard an ominous thunderclap when I closed the book and started considering what the status quo going into the next book would be. I was really worried we were entering a 'War Arc Naruto' type of story. (reviewed 6-15-2026)

title: Ender's Game
review: This is my go-to reccomendation for people who want to read more. It's short, moves very quick, has fun ideas, and is well written. Humanity was attacked by an insect-like alien race. They killed thousands of humans but were driven away by a mysterious attack given by one human. Now, humanity wants to take the fight to them before the aliens can regroup. So they start a dangerous military training school, and Ender rises to the top with his extreme tactical genius. There's lots of great sequences in here. One standout is Ender telling his teammates in a zero gravity combat excersise to stop thinking in Earth terms. Think of the enemy base as 'down' and use your legs to shield from the enemy stunners. Again this book is really short and moves really quick. I highly reccomend it. (reviewed 6-15-2026)

title: Speaker for the Dead (technically the sequel to Ender's Game)
review: This is the book Orson Scott Card always wanted to write, but felt he needed to write Ender's Game as a sort of prologue. The twist at the end of Ender's Game was supposed to be the opening to this book. Then he wrote Ender's Game and it became a smash hit. This is very funny because this book is nothing like Ender's Game so all of that book's fans are in for some serious whiplash. Ender's Game is short and pacey, this is slow and thoughtful. It's about Ender being the 'Speaker for the Dead', where he gives honest euolgies for people who have died. He tells the whole truth about someone's life, the good and the bad./n/n I will briefly mention this book is explicitly anti-Catholic (a prominient character is a bishop). It hates Hagiography (recording of saints lives) because of its tendancy to erase flaws in the person's life and create ficticious virtuous acts. This all feels really silly to me. Hagiography happens to all historical figures years after their death. People become closer to myth with time. Maybe I'm not engaging the book on its terms but all the anti-hagiography stuff felt soap-boxy to me./n/nFun Fact: this was the first book I read where relativity is a central plot element. If you can travel to another planet, it will be like two months for you, but might be 15 years for everyone else. Ender agrees to give a eulogy for a little girls dad who just died, but by the time he gets there the whole family has grown up. The now grown woman wishes she'd never called for Ender, and we see the brokenness the whole family suffered from their father even a decade after he passed./n/nIf you liked Ender's Game, and a slow thoughtful exploration of both the ending to that book, and the whole concept of a 'Speaker for the Dead' sounds intriguing I'd pick it up. Just realize I think the book is more than twice as long. (reviewed 6-15-2026)

title: A Wizard of Earthsea (Earthsea Book 1)
review: Le Guin feels like no other fantasy writer from her time or now because she is so minimal. Read a chapter of The Wheel of Time then read a Le Guin chapter and you'll instantly feel it. Le Guin leaves so much up to your imaginination. Robert Jordan will describe with detail the dark columns of the room and the shafts of light falling across the red and blue carpet. Le Guin will just say 'the grand hall' with maybe one more load bearing desriptive word. So much of the world is never described but felt. There are these wizards who sail across by summoning the wind, they go and help the small towns like some wandering sage. And of course our protagonist is hunted by their own shadow that they foolishly called into the world. Without exact description Le Guin paints a world full of flavor./n/nMy favorite chapter in the book is when the protagonist fights a dragon. They can't overpower the dragon, but they have used their magic to determine the dragon's true name, giving them power over it. But speaking the true name requires speaking in the old tongue. The wizard cannot lie, however the this is the language of the dragons 'It is their own language, and they can lie in it, twisting the true words to false ends, catching the unwary hearer in a maze of mirrorwords each of which reflects the truth and none of which leads anywhere.' The wizard must resist the deals and temptations of the dragon, until the dragon finally is wrangled, and sent far away from the island./n/nYou see why I love this book so much. It feels so different from the rest of fantasy.
